title:
Dual first-line maintenance by PARP inhibitor and bevacizumab can
cause confusion in high-grade serous ovarian cancer: A case of PRES and a review
of the literature
case_prompt: A 70-year-old woman with FIGO stage IVB high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma received six cycles of neoadjuvant carboplatin/paclitaxel followed by interval debulking surgery, then maintenance bevacizumab (10 cycles) and olaparib without hypertension or proteinuria. Sixteen days after her 10th bevacizumab infusion, she was admitted with urinary incontinence, grade 2 asthenia, and acute confusion. On exam her Glasgow Coma Score was 14; vital signs were normal, and the rest of the neurologic exam was unremarkable. She had no history of seizures or neurologic disease. Laboratory studies, urine and blood cultures, ECG, and chest radiograph were all normal. Noncontrast head CT showed no hemorrhage and no abnormalities in the posterior circulation. Lumbar puncture was negative for infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic cells. Empiric ceftriaxone was started. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral high signal intensity in the cortex and subcortical white matter of the posterior parietal and occipital lobes on FLAIR images, without diffusion restriction; ADC values were increased, indicating vasogenic edema.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome was considered but excluded because CTA did not show any abnormality in the posterior circulation — “Cerebral CT angiography (CTA) did not show any abnormality regarding the size of the posterior circulation arteries, which ruled out RCVS.”  
2. Infectious meningitis was considered but excluded because the lumbar puncture was negative for infectious disease — “The lumbar puncture was negative for infectious, inflammatory and neoplastic diseases.”  
3. Meningeal carcinomatosis was considered but excluded because the lumbar puncture was negative for neoplastic disease — “The lumbar puncture was negative for infectious, inflammatory and neoplastic diseases.”  
4. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome was supported by the MRI findings of bilateral posterior cortical and subcortical vasogenic edema without restricted diffusion — “Axial fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images showed high signal intensities involving the cortex and the subcortical white matter in the posterior parietal and occipital regions bilaterally without restricted diffusion, consistent with vasogenic edema and highly suggestive of PRES.”
